enrichment.short_title: Iraqi Kurdish temporary admission after section 67
key_facts: Ashraf Khadir, an Iraqi Kurdish illegal entrant, was refused asylum and removal directions were issued but he could not be returned to the Kurdish Autonomous Area.
Crane J quashed the Secretary of State's refusal of exceptional leave to remain, holding removal was no longer pending and temporary admission was unavailable.
Parliament enacted section 67 of the 2002 Act during the appeal, deeming a person liable to detention for temporary admission where practical difficulties delay removal arrangements.
The Court of Appeal held section 67 applied retrospectively to the appeal and allowed the Secretary of State's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a judicial review quashing the refusal of exceptional leave to remain; cross-appeal seeking mandatory exceptional leave.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; the Secretary of State need not reconsider exceptional leave to remain.
enrichment.ratio: Section 67(3) of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 retrospectively deems a person whose removal is impeded by practical difficulties to be liable to detention for the purposes of temporary admission under paragraph 21 of Schedule 2 to the Immigration Act 1971, so the Secretary of State may lawfully refuse exceptional leave and maintain temporary admission status.
legal_issues: Whether removal remains pending when return to northern Iraq is impracticable
Application of Hardial Singh and Tan Te Lam principles to temporary admission
Retrospective effect of section 67 on pending appeals
Whether Article 6 ECHR applies to immigration status decisions

enrichment.short_title: Far East civilian internee ex-gratia birth criteria upheld

statutes_considered.title: British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act 1914

key_facts: ABCIFER challenged the Government's £10,000 ex-gratia scheme for British civilians interned by Japan in the Second World War.
Dr Moonie announced the scheme in November 2000 but later clarified eligibility required the claimant or a parent or grandparent to have been born in the United Kingdom.
Many British subjects born in the Far East who had lived in the UK since the war were refused payment under the birth criteria.
Scott Baker J dismissed the judicial review and the Court of Appeal upheld the scheme as rational and not an abuse of legitimate expectation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of a judicial review challenge to a non-statutory ex-gratia compensation scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; birth criteria and strong-links policy held lawful.
enrichment.ratio: It was not irrational for the Government to limit ex-gratia payments to British civilian internees with strong UK links demonstrated by UK birth of the claimant, parent or grandparent, and Dr Moonie's November 2000 announcement did not create a clear and unequivocal legitimate expectation that all British subjects at internment would qualify.
legal_issues: Wednesbury irrationality of strong-links and birth criteria
Whether proportionality applies outside ECHR and EU law
Legitimate expectation and conspicuous unfairness
Whether ex-gratia entitlement is a possession under Article 1 First Protocol

enrichment.short_title: Juvenile HMP detainee tariff review duty
key_facts: Maria Rossi (formerly Maria Smith) was detained during Her Majesty's pleasure after a juvenile murder conviction with a 15-year tariff set in 1993.
Following Venables, the Secretary of State re-fixed her tariff at 13 years but adopted a transitional policy refusing further tariff reviews after the Lord Chief Justice's recommendation.
The claimant sought judicial review arguing Venables requires ongoing Secretary of State review of minimum terms for section 53(1) detainees sentenced before 30 November 2000.
Kennedy LJ and Mitchell J held the policy unlawful and that section 28(4) requires the Secretary of State to keep open the possibility of further review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim challenging the Secretary of State's transitional policy on tariff review for juvenile offenders detained during Her Majesty's pleasure.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded in part; unlawful policy identified and relief granted requiring the Secretary of State to keep open the possibility of further tariff review.
enrichment.ratio: For offenders sentenced to detention during Her Majesty's pleasure under section 53(1) of the Children and Young Persons Act 1933 before tariffs were judicially set, the Secretary of State retains a continuing duty under section 28(4) of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997 to keep open the possibility of reducing the minimum term in light of the detainee's progress and section 44 welfare obligations, as established in Venables.
legal_issues: Continuing Secretary of State duty to review HMP minimum terms
Effect of section 82A on pre-2000 juvenile murder sentences
Whether ex parte A affects custody character of non-secure local authority remand
Application of Venables to Secretary of State-set tariffs

enrichment.short_title: Retirement gratuity not capped by later regulations
key_facts: Mrs Nicholls, an ILEA school cleaner from 1982, had a contractual retirement gratuity of two weeks' pay per year of service.
Greenwich Council paid only £1,171.94 on retirement in 2000, relying on Local Government (Discretionary Payments) Regulations 1996 caps interpreted via Allsop.
The employment tribunal and EAT held the regulations prevented payment of the full contractual gratuity.
The Court of Appeal held the regulations do not retrospectively deprive vested contractual rights and Allsop is distinguishable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against employment tribunal and EAT decisions rejecting a breach of contract claim for unpaid retirement gratuity.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; council liable for £2,903.64 damages for breach of contract.
enrichment.ratio: Regulations made under section 7 of the Superannuation Act 1972 are not framed to operate retrospectively so as to cap payment of a retirement gratuity validly promised in a pre-regulations contract of employment that did not exceed the statutory maximum in force when the contract was made.
legal_issues: Retrospective effect of superannuation regulations on vested contractual rights
Whether Allsop precludes enforcement of pre-regulations gratuity terms
Construction of section 112 Local Government Act 1972 appointment terms
Presumption against retrospective impairment of private rights

enrichment.short_title: Mother's mortgage undue influence but bank not liable
key_facts: Mrs Chater, aged about 61, mortgaged her home jointly with her son Andrew for over £34,000 to fund his laser printing franchise.
The county court judge found undue influence and misrepresentation by the son but held the bank was not put on inquiry and upheld possession and debt judgment.

Following Etridge (No 2), the Court of Appeal found the transaction called for explanation and undue influence was established, but the bank faced a joint application without signs the loan was solely for the son's business.
The appeal was dismissed because the lender was not put on inquiry and took no unreasonable steps obligation arose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a county court order for possession and judgment on a mortgage secured by undue influence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; mortgage enforceable against Mrs Chater despite undue influence by her son.
enrichment.ratio: Where a mother and son apply jointly for a remortgage on the mother's home without information that the advance is solely for the son's commercial purposes, a bank is not put on inquiry as to undue influence under Etridge (No 2) and need not require independent legal advice before enforcing the security.
legal_issues: Presumption of undue influence in parent-child mortgage transactions
Whether transaction calls for explanation under Etridge
Bank put on inquiry for joint borrower applications
Causation of misrepresentation as to loan amount

enrichment.short_title: Hague Rules package limit applies to deck breach

statutes_considered.title: Hague Rules (International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law relating to Bills of Lading 1924)

key_facts: Thirty-four excavators were shipped underdeck from Korea but restowed on deck in China without cargo interests' consent and eight were lost in heavy weather.
The contract required underdeck carriage and incorporated the Hague Rules as enacted in Turkey.
Hirst J in The Chanda held unauthorised deck stowage disentitled the carrier from Article IV rule 5 limitation.
The Court of Appeal overruled The Chanda and held the words 'in any event' in rule 5 apply even to serious breach of an underdeck obligation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on preliminary issues in a cargo claim, declining to follow The Chanda on Hague Rules limitation for unauthorised deck carriage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; carrier may rely on Article IV rule 5 package limitation despite breach of underdeck stowage obligation.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Hague Rules 1924, the phrase 'in any event' in Article IV rule 5 gives the carrier package limitation even where cargo is carried on deck in breach of a contractual underdeck obligation; the deviation cases and warehouse cases do not displace this construction.
legal_issues: Whether unauthorised deck stowage is quasi-deviation excluding limitation
Construction of 'in any event' in Article IV rule 5
Whether The Chanda should be followed
Relationship between Article III rule 6 time bar and rule 5 limitation

enrichment.short_title: Unsafe child abuse convictions after judge interventions
key_facts: The appellant was convicted of two indecent assaults and rape of his niece V, then aged 6 to 10, with an 8-year sentence.
V had learning difficulties and gave evidence by video link; medical evidence showed repetitive penetration inconsistent with her account of only three incidents.
The trial judge intervened during cross-examination, told V she knew the answer about prior sexual intercourse, and summing-up misdirected on medical evidence and consent.
The Divisional Court quashed the convictions as unsafe but ordered a retrial given the seriousness of the allegations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against convictions for indecent assault and rape of a child witness.
enrichment.outcome: Convictions quashed as unsafe; retrial ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge's interventions during a vulnerable child's evidence and a summing-up that misstates medical evidence and gives an unnecessary consent direction may lead the jury to believe the judge favoured the prosecution, convictions are unsafe even if the case was weak and the jury deliberated for many hours.
legal_issues: Judicial interventions rendering trial unfair
Summing-up on medical evidence of repetitive penetration
Whether consent direction was material in child rape trial
Principles from Matthews on unsafe convictions

key_facts: Mr Krayem, a Palestinian born in Kuwait living in a UNRWA camp in Lebanon, claimed asylum in the UK in 1997.
His fear of an armed group and general discrimination against Palestinians in Lebanese UNRWA camps was rejected on credibility and persecution grounds.
Expert evidence from George Joffé described systemic discrimination in employment, housing and security for camp residents.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal rejected Joffé's generalised views but gave inadequate reasons for why discrimination would not amount to persecution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissal of an asylum appeal on persecution in Lebanon.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision quashed and appeal remitted to a differently constituted tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tribunal rejects expert and objective evidence that Palestinian refugees in UNRWA camps face discrimination capable of amounting to persecution under Hathaway's third category of rights, it must give adequate reasons explaining whether such treatment is incapable of constituting persecution or is insufficiently serious, not merely assert that UNRWA care cannot breach UN conventions.
legal_issues: Whether economic and social discrimination can amount to persecution
Adequacy of tribunal reasons rejecting Joffé expert evidence
Application of Hathaway sustained systemic denial of state protection test
Status of Palestinian without nationality under Refugee Convention

enrichment.short_title: Default judgment upheld after debt admissions
key_facts: ED&F Man sued Mahesh Patel and a partner for US$283,860 for two alcohol shipments to Kazakhstan under a 1995 joint venture agreement.
Default judgment was entered against Patel who argued the joint venture terms still governed and payment was not due until Quickstop received proceeds from on-sales.
From 1998 to 2001 Patel repeatedly acknowledged the debt, proposed repayment schedules and made partial payments without citing the joint venture defence.
The High Court and Court of Appeal held the written admissions showed abandonment of joint venture accounting and no real prospect of defending the claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal to set aside default judgment under CPR 13.3(1)(a) for alcohol supply debt.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; default judgment stands against the first defendant.
enrichment.ratio: On an application to set aside default judgment, repeated unqualified written acknowledgments of debt and partial payments by a sophisticated businessman, made with knowledge of the facts and without reserving a joint-venture defence, demonstrate no real prospect of successfully defending the claim even where disputed contractual terms might otherwise require trial.
legal_issues: CPR 13.3 real prospect of success vs CPR 24.2 summary judgment test
Whether Saudi Eagle higher threshold applies to setting aside default judgment
Effect of post-contract admissions on joint venture defence
Mini-trial on set-aside application where admissions exist

enrichment.short_title: Youth remand escape from lawful custody upheld
key_facts: A 15-year-old appellant was remanded to local authority accommodation without a secure accommodation requirement under section 23 of the 1969 Act.
Youth offending team practitioner Alex Cooter collected him from court cells and told him not to move while she sought access to the office; he absconded.
Magistrates convicted him of common law escape from lawful custody.
Gage J held he was in lawful custody at the moment of absconding because section 23(3) empowered detention and Cooter was exercising control over his movement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from youth court conviction for escape from lawful custody.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction for escape from lawful custody upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A young person remanded to local authority accommodation under section 23 of the Children and Young Persons Act 1969 may be in lawful custody when a person acting for the designated authority exercises section 23(3) power to detain him, such that absconding while under direct control and told not to move constitutes escape from lawful custody even without a secure accommodation order.
legal_issues: Whether non-secure section 23 remand is custodial in nature
Application of ex parte A to escape prosecutions
Section 23(3) detention power vs section 32 arrest for absentees
Whether telling a youth not to move constitutes lawful custody
